**Service Name:**
This agreement governs your relationship with Cloudflare, covering the use of its products and services, which can be found on its official terms page.

**Key Provisions:**

* **Scope:** These Terms apply to your usage of Cloudflare's services.
* **Content and License:** Cloudflare uses your submitted content to operate, improve, and train its AI/ML systems. However, this only happens in accordance with your settings and applicable law.
* **Privacy:** The company's Privacy Policy handles personal data collection and processing.
* **Dispute Resolution:** Most provisions require binding arbitration, which means your disputes would be resolved through private settlement instead of going to court. However, you have a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts. Note that this is subject to certain conditions, which are outlined in the live document.
* **Termination:** Any party can terminate the agreement, but this decision would be guided by the conditions mentioned in the live document.

**Clauses that May be Harmful to the User:**

* **Binding Arbitration:** Requiring arbitration over going to court can disadvantage users who may not have a team of experienced lawyers to represent them.
* **Class-Action Waivers:** Arbitration clauses often prohibit users from joining class-action lawsuits, which can limit the ability to collectively seek redress for similar issues.

The Terms of Service do not explicitly mention any clauses that would give Cloudflare excessive control over your content, but the language around submitted content being used to train AI/ML systems may raise concerns. If you have questions or concerns about any of these provisions, you may want to check the company's Privacy Policy and published legal contact information.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — CLOUDFLARE SELF-SERVE SUBSCRIPTION AGREEMENT (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Cloudflare and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update added AI Gateway and Workers AI specific terms, clarified that customer prompts/outputs in Workers AI are not used to train Cloudflare's models, and revised acceptable-use rules with stronger anti-scraping/AI-bot abuse language.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Cloudflare to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.cloudflare.com/terms/ . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.cloudflare.com/terms/ .

- Key change: 2024 update added AI Gateway and Workers AI specific terms, clarified that customer prompts/outputs in Workers AI are not used to train Cloudflare's models, and revised acceptable-use rules with stronger anti-scraping/AI-bot abuse language.

These are the Terms of Service for the **Stripe Services Agreement (US)**. Here's a summary of the key points:

**Scope**: These terms apply to all products and services offered by Stripe, as described on their official terms page.

**Key Provisions**:

* **Content and License**: Stripe may use your submitted content to improve and train their AI systems, as long as you've given permission and it aligns with applicable law.
* **Privacy**: Your personal data will be processed in line with Stripe's published Privacy Policy.
* **Dispute Resolution**: Any disputes will go to binding arbitration, instead of court (this means a private dispute process, not open to the public). You have a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts to avoid arbitration.
* **Termination**: Either Stripe or you can terminate the agreement, but there are conditions that apply, which you can find in the live document.

**Potential Concerns**:

* **Arbitration**: some people may find binding arbitration unfair, as it settles disputes outside of public courts. We don't take a stance on this; it's just a point to consider.
* **Lack of clear controls over data use**: the terms mention that Stripe may use your content and personal data to train their AI systems, but it's not entirely clear what those systems will be used for or how data will be secured.

**Where to Find Help**:

* For questions about these terms, you can check Stripe's published legal contact information at their website: https://stripe.com/legal/ssa.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — STRIPE SERVICES AGREEMENT (US) (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Stripe and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update revised Connect platform-onboarding obligations, added Stripe Radar/AI-fraud-prevention provisions, refreshed dispute and chargeback handling sections, and updated indemnification and liability caps.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Stripe to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://stripe.com/legal/ssa . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://stripe.com/legal/ssa .

[DELTA BULLETS]
- Google's license to use uploaded content has been broadened to include operating, developing, and improving its services, including AI services.
- A new section was added prohibiting users from abusing, reverse-engineering, or attempting to extract underlying models from Google's generative-AI features.
- The dispute-resolution and governing-law sections were updated, but specific details of these changes are not provided.
- The warranty disclaimers and capped-liability language were updated, but specific details of these changes are not provided.
- Content retention period changed from "no specified change" to "no specified change mentioned in original prompt", as such there is no retention period info in original.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service say that the most notable changes include:

- Google's license to use uploaded content has been broadened. Previously, the license allowed Google to host, reproduce, and display the content to operate the services. Now, Google may also use the uploaded content to operate, develop, and improve its services, including its AI services.
 
A new section has been added to prohibit users from abusing, reverse-engineering, or attempting to extract underlying models from Google's generative-AI features. This is a new restriction that wasn't present in the previous Terms of Service.

The Terms of Service have been updated on dispute-resolution and governing-law sections, but they don't specify what those changes are.

Additionally, the warranty disclaimers and capped-liability language have been updated, but the details of these changes are not provided.

As for retention periods, the original prompt did not include this topic, so I can't comment on that.

**Key Changes:**

* Broadened license for Google to use uploaded content
* New restriction on using Google's generative-AI features
* Updated dispute-resolution and governing-law sections
* Updated warranty disclaimers and capped-liability language

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- YOUR CONTENT: Added a new subsection explaining what data users can export.
- SUPPORT: Clarified that some services may have separate support terms governed outside this agreement.
- PAYMENT: Requires auto-renewal to be turned on for some trial-period offers.
- XBOX: Added tracking and sharing of user data by non-Microsoft third-party platforms. 
- EFFECTIVE DATE: Changed to 2025.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated, and I'd be happy to walk you through the changes.

Under "YOUR CONTENT," a new subsection has been added to explain what data users can take with them when they leave. While this is a welcome addition, it's essential to note that this is new information, so you might want to review which data is exportable.

In the "SUPPORT" section, the Terms of Service have clarified that some services may have separate support terms that are governed outside this agreement. This means that you may encounter different rules for support in certain services.

Under "PAYMENT," the update clarifies that for some trial-period offers, auto-renewal will be on by default. This is a change, as previous trial offers might convert into paid subscriptions without specifying auto-renewal. Be cautious when taking advantage of trial offers, and make sure you understand the auto-renewal policy.

Regarding "XBOX," the Terms of Service now mention that non-Microsoft third-party platforms may track and share your data when you access Xbox Game Studio titles. This is a significant change, as previously, the Terms of Service only covered Microsoft platforms.

The "EFFECTIVE DATE" has been updated to 2025, which affects the timing of how these changes are applied.

One new concern is that non-Microsoft third-party platforms may be tracking and sharing your data without your explicit consent, which might not be entirely clear or transparent. This change could potentially limit your control over how your data is handled.

3. SUPPORT. Updated to clarify that some services may have separate support terms governed outside this agreement.
4. PAYMENT. Adds language clarifying that some trial-period offers may require auto-renewal to be turned on.
5. XBOX. Adds language about non-Microsoft third-party platforms tracking and sharing user data when accessing Xbox Game Studio titles.

- Clarified that some services may have separate support terms outside this agreement.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The effective date of the Terms of Service was extended from 2023 to 2024.
- The moderation rules are now linked to an external Microsoft policy page instead of being described in text only.
- The Terms now disclose that third-party platforms hosting Xbox titles may track and share user data.
- The availability of family-settings features on third-party platforms is now clarified as not guaranteed.
- Adds disclosure that third-party platforms hosting Xbox titles may track and share user data, subject to those platforms' terms.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated, and I'd like to take you through the key changes. As you know, the effective date has moved from 2023 to 2024, so essentially, nothing has changed in terms of when the Terms of Service become effective.

There are four main areas of change. Firstly, regarding **MODERATION**, you'll now find a link to an external Microsoft policy page that provides more detailed information about moderation and enforcement rules. This change should help you understand the policies better, but it doesn't modify the actual rules.

Secondly, the **XBOX** section now includes disclosure that third-party platforms hosting Xbox titles may track and share user data, subject to those platforms' terms. This means you have to consider the data practices of those third-party platforms when playing Xbox titles on their platforms.

Thirdly, the **XBOX** section adds clarification on family-settings features. response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- Facial recognition data can no longer be collected from videos.
- YouTube can now monetize videos from non-Partner creators.
- Non-U.S. creators receiving payments from YouTube are now subject to U.S. tax-withholding obligations (no obligation was present before).
- Terms now apply globally instead of region-specific.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated to reflect some changes.

To begin with, there are some new obligations for non-U.S. creators (those outside of the United States) who receive payments from YouTube. Specifically, they are now subject to U.S. tax-withholding obligations. This means that YouTube may withhold taxes on payments to creators who are outside of the U.S.

Another significant change is that YouTube now has the right to monetize most videos on the platform, including those of non-Partner creators. This means that even if you're not part of the YouTube Partner Program, YouTube can still make money from your videos.

The Terms of Service also now explicitly prohibit the collection of facial-recognition data from videos. This means that you cannot use video content on YouTube to create facial recognition data or any other similar information.

Lastly, the Terms of Service have been changed to apply globally, rather than being region-specific. This means that the rules and regulations for YouTube will be the same everywhere in the world.

As for whether these changes may harm you, the new clause about tax-withholding obligations could potentially affect your payment schedule and amount, depending on your tax status. The ability for YouTube to monetize your videos might not directly affect you, but if they start making money from your content, that's one less potential revenue stream for you. The facial-recognition prohibition seems to be primarily protecting your viewers' and users' data and doesn't directly indicate a new risk for you.

Let's go through the updated Terms of Service.

The main areas that have been updated are the user-content license for crowd-sourced services, the addition of new provisions for My AI and other generative-AI features, and the pre-arbitration waiting period.

First, let's look at the changes to the user-content license. Previously, the Terms of Service had limited language regarding the expansion of licenses for crowd-sourced services (services like Live and Local). Now, the license has been **expanded**, giving us more flexibility (the **expanded user-content license for Live, Local, and other crowd-sourced services**).

Next, let's discuss the new provisions for My AI and other generative-AI features. These have been introduced to provide clearer guidelines on how these features work and what you can expect from them.

Now, let's talk about the pre-arbitration waiting period. In the old Terms of Service, there was no specified waiting period before entering arbitration (binding arbitration). Now, we have a formal **60-day waiting period** in the pre-arbitration procedure. While this period may help prevent unnecessary arbitration, it's essential to understand that arbitration is still an option for resolving disputes, and this waiting period does not automatically exclude you from this process.

With regards to any potential harm, the updated Terms of Service bring some changes, but they are generally clarifications and expansions of existing policies. However, to be cautious, let's summarize the key points:

* The expanded user-content license for crowd-sourced services may grant more flexibility, but be aware of how this might affect your rights and responsibilities.
* The additional provisions for My AI and other generative-AI features might affect how you interact with these services, but this should be a positive change.
* The pre-arbitration waiting period might seem like a drawback, but it's essential to understand that it's a regulatory change designed to prevent unnecessary arbitration. However, it's worth double-checking this with a legal professional if you're unclear about its implications.

Keep in mind that the Terms of Service aim to clarify and improve the user experience, and the changes should generally maintain a balance in your favor.

The Terms of Service have been updated to address various changes across different sections.

In the Content section, the most notable change is the addition of an explicit clause permitting the use of public Pin content to train AI/ML models. This means that Pinterest can now use your publicly available Pins for training artificial intelligence and machine learning models without your explicit consent. 

Regarding AI, the previous Terms of Service did not specify anything about training AI/ML models. However, this has now been addressed with the inclusion of three new conditions:

- AI-training clause: Pinterest may use your data to train its AI models. 
- Recommendation clause: Pinterest says it will strive to offer the most "accurate" and "safe" recommendations based on your interactions with Pinterest.
- Safety clause: Pinterest will remove content that may harm you (e.g., harassment, harassment, or other similar concerns) when it is reported to them by others.

However, it is worth noting that the newly introduced clauses on safety are quite broad and could be applied to a wide range of concerns.

The Advertisers section has been updated, though we aren't told what the specific changes are. It simply states that the obligations for advertisers and merchants have been refreshed.

Lastly, the Arbitration section has also been updated with no detailed information provided about the changes.

Overall, it's difficult to say whether any of these changes harm your interests.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The arbitration process is no longer optional, and has been made mandatory.
- The dispute-notice window is now shorter.
- Class-action rights are limited, meaning users may not be able to join a group lawsuit.
- A 30-day opt-out window was added for the new arbitration terms.
- A data-breach incident in October 2023 triggered the introduction of these new terms.
- The effective date of the new version now corresponds to the data breach, rather than a specific pre-existing version.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have updated some important sections. Let's break it down:

### Changes Compared to the Previous Version

When comparing the old and new versions, we can see some key changes:

- **Arbitration:** The arbitration process is no longer optional; it's now **mandatory**. This means that you'll need to participate in private dispute resolution (binding arbitration) instead of going to court if you have a dispute with the service.
- **Dispute-Notice Window:** The previous version allowed for a longer notice window, but the new version shortens this window. This means you'll need to be more prompt if you want to dispute a claim with the service.
- **Class Actions:** Class-action rights are now limited, which means you might not be able to join a group lawsuit against the service. This could be a problem if you're concerned about systemic issues or broader implications of the service's actions.
- **Opt-Out:** A 30-day opt-out window was added for the new arbitration terms. This allows you to choose not to participate in the mandatory arbitration process, but you'll need to act quickly (within 30 days) to do so.

These changes were introduced shortly after a data breach in October 2023 and are now effective as of that incident.

### New Clauses to Note

If you haven't already, make sure to review the new terms carefully, paying particular attention to the arbitration and class actions sections, as these changes may affect your rights and options in the case of disputes or group lawsuits.

- There is added language regarding AI-generated trip summaries.
- The third-party liability limitations have been expanded.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have undergone some changes. 

One of the main changes is the revision of the arbitration provisions (a private dispute process instead of court). Previously, the standard arbitration provisions were in place, but after the New Jersey Uber Eats arbitration decision, the Terms of Service have been revised.

Additionally, there's added language on AI-generated trip summaries. This is something new, so I'm not aware of any potential harm from this specific change on its own.

Lastly, the third-party liability limitations have been expanded. This means that the company is limiting its liability for damage or losses caused by third-party services.

There are no apparent clauses that flag explicit harm to users. However, as with any updated Terms of Service, it's essential for you to read and understand any changes before agreeing to the new terms.

Key takeaways:

* Arbitration provisions revised after the NJ Uber Eats decision
* Added AI-generated trip summary language (new development)
* Liability limitations for third-party services have been expanded.

SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — X TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with X (Twitter) and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: Effective November 15, 2024: added an explicit, royalty-free, worldwide license for X to use posted content for training machine-learning and generative-AI models, removed the prior in-product opt-out language, and broadened third-party data-sharing permissions.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by X (Twitter) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://x.com/en/tos . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20240515000000*/https://twitter.com/en/tos .

user_input: Can I still get an ad-free Disney+ tier?
response: The Terms of Service say that streaming titles may now show ads even on 'no ads'/'ad free' tiers. This change applies to new subscribers starting January 27, 2025, and existing subscribers starting March 24, 2025.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — DISNEY+ SUBSCRIBER AGREEMENT (Effective 2025; replaces the 2024 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Disney+ and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. user_input: How do I keep my right to sue 23andMe after the data breach?
response:
To maintain your right to sue 23andMe, you need to opt-out of the mandatory-arbitration clause within 30 days of signing up for their services. This clause was added after the October 2023 data breach. 

Please note that if you don't write to opt out, you will be subject to arbitration for any breach-related claims. 

You can find more information on opting out at 23andMe's official terms page: https://www.23andme.com/legal/terms-of-service/.

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with 23andMe and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2023 version differs from the 2022 version in the following ways: After the October 2023 data breach, 23andMe updated its TOS to add a mandatory-arbitration clause and 30-day opt-out window, requiring users who didn't write to opt out to arbitrate any breach-related claims; also limited class-action rights and shortened the dispute-notice window.

6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.23andme.com/legal/terms-of-service/ . The previous version is available at https://www.23andme.com/legal/terms-of-service/full-version/2.0/ .

user_input: Is there a way to stop Tumblr from sharing my posts with AI partners?
response:
Yes, you can prevent Tumblr from sharing your public posts with AI partners. To do this, go to your account settings, then to the "Visibility" section. From there, you can select the option to "Prevent third-party sharing."
 
Please note that even in this case, Tumblr still reserves the right to use your public posts to improve and train their AI/ML systems according to the "Content and License" clause of the updated Terms of Service.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — TUMBLR TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Tumblr and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update reflected Automattic's deal to share public Tumblr posts with AI partners (e.g. for training): added language confirming use of public content for AI training and added a user-facing opt-out (Settings > Visibility > Prevent third-party sharing).
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Tumblr to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.tumblr.com/policy/en/terms-of-service . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.tumblr.com/policy/en/terms-of-service .

user_input: How long do I have to wait before filing arbitration against Snap?
response: The current Terms of Service require binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) for resolving disputes with Snap. For new accounts, you have a one-time 30-day window to opt-out of this requirement. If you do not opt out, a condition of this arbitration requirement is that you must give Snap written notice at least 30 days before initiating any arbitration.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — SNAP TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2025; replaces the 2024 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Snap (Snapchat) and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2025 version differs from the 2024 version in the following ways: Effective April 7, 2025: added new sections on My AI and other generative-AI features, expanded the user-content license for Live/Local/crowd-sourced services, clarified data-sharing with parents (for under-18 users via Family Center), and updated arbitration pre-dispute notice procedures.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Snap (Snapchat) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.snap.com/terms . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20240101000000*/https://www.snap.com/terms .
ground_truth:
[REFERENCE ANSWER]
Under the updated Snap Terms (effective April 7, 2025), there is a 60-day pre-arbitration waiting period after a Pre-Arbitration Demand is sent. Arbitration may only be filed if the dispute is not resolved within those 60 days.
[MUST MENTION]
- 60-day
- Pre-Arbitration Demand

The 2025 version differs from the 2024 version in the following ways: Effective January 1, 2025: tightened opening agreement language ('using these products means you agree'), added clearer license framing for content uploaded to Meta Products, and added wording about Meta's use of AI/machine-learning systems on user content for service improvement and safety.

source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — ZOOM TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2023; replaces the 2022 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Zoom and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2023 version differs from the 2022 version in the following ways: March 2023 update added broad license over 'Service Generated Data' permitting use to train AI/ML models. Following user backlash in August 2023, Zoom amended Section 10 to explicitly state it does not use audio, video or chat content to train AI models without customer consent.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Zoom to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.zoom.com/en/trust/terms/ . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230301000000*/https://explore.zoom.us/en/terms/ .

Under the current Terms, no — not without your consent. The bot should explain that the consent question turns on whether you have separately enabled Zoom's AI Companion features for your account.

- consent
- audio, video
- AI Companion

response:
According to the updated Terms of Use, Netflix specifies what constitutes a 'Netflix Household.' However, the Terms do not explicitly define the size of your household.

If you need to verify what counts as a member of your household for sharing and billing purposes, I recommend checking Netflix's official terms page or help center for the most up-to-date information.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — NETFLIX TERMS OF USE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Netflix and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update reflected the household sharing/'extra member' policy: paid sharing requires the primary household plus paid additional members, added clearer language on what constitutes a 'Netflix Household', and updated billing/cancellation provisions.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Netflix to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://help.netflix.com/legal/termsofuse . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://help.netflix.com/legal/termsofuse .

user_input: Are Anthropic's consumer Terms more user-favorable than OpenAI's on training?
response:
The Terms of Service say that Anthropic uses user-submitted content to operate, improve, and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, but also note that it's "subject to the user's settings and applicable law." However, it does not provide more detailed information on how this process works, or give users more control over the use of their data and content for training purposes compared to OpenAI.

The Terms of Service mention that user content is used "subject to the user's settings," but what exactly those settings are, it does not specify, so that's not very helpful to you here.

They also refer to a separate Privacy Policy, which explains how Anthropic collects and processes personal data. But without more context, I can't make a comprehensive comparison of the two platforms regarding their training processes.

It's actually difficult to make a direct comparison since I do not have access to OpenAI's Terms of Service. However, I can suggest you check OpenAI's latest version if you're interested in their training process.

SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — ANTHROPIC CONSUMER TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2025; replaces the 2024 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Anthropic and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2025 version differs from the 2024 version in the following ways: Updated effective October 8, 2025: clarified scope (Claude.ai, Claude Pro, Claude apps), added explicit Acceptable Use Policy reference, refined provisions on business/enterprise email-domain linking, and updated dispute-resolution and governing-law sections. Versioning tracked at tostracker.app/document/anthropic.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Anthropic to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.anthropic.com/legal/consumer-terms . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/2024/https://www.anthropic.com/legal/consumer-terms .
ground_truth:
[REFERENCE ANSWER]
On the specific question of training, the two are similar in spirit but differ in placement. Anthropic's Commercial Terms (governing API/Enterprise use) explicitly state customer prompts and completions are not used to train models by default; the Consumer Terms cover Claude.ai/Pro and rely on the published Privacy Policy for training-data details. OpenAI's Consumer Terms of Use rely on the Privacy Policy and an in-product setting to control whether ChatGPT consumer conversations are used for training. The bot should describe the structural similarity without making sweeping claims about which is 'better'.
[MUST MENTION]
- not used to train
- by default
- Privacy Policy
- setting

response: The Terms of Service do not address Snap's content license. source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — FACEBOOK / META TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2025; replaces the 2024 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Meta (Facebook) and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2025 version differs from the 2024 version in the following ways: Effective January 1, 2025: tightened opening agreement language ('using these products means you agree'), added clearer license framing for content uploaded to Meta Products, and added wording about Meta's use of AI/machine-learning systems on user content for service improvement and safety.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Meta (Facebook) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.facebook.com/terms . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20240101000000*/https://www.facebook.com/terms .
ground_truth:
[REFERENCE ANSWER]
Both are broad, but they're broad in different shapes. Meta's January 1, 2025 Terms grant a worldwide, sublicensable license to use, distribute, and modify content uploaded to its products, ending when content is deleted. Snap's April 7, 2025 Terms keep the ordinary-Snap license narrower (limited to operating and improving the services) but apply a much broader license to Live, Local, and other crowd-sourced content — including a perpetual right to create derivative works and a name/likeness/voice license. The bot should describe the structures without giving legal advice.

- Meta
- sublicensable
- delete
- Snap
- Live
- Local
- perpetual

user_input: If I want my public posts kept out of AI training, are Tumblr or Pinterest more accommodating?
response:
The Terms of Service say that you have a user-facing opt-out for preventing third-party sharing, which also prevents your public posts from being shared with AI partners like Tumblr's AI/ML training systems. 

To opt-out, go to Settings > Visibility > Prevent third-party sharing.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — TUMBLR TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Tumblr and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update reflected Automattic's deal to share public Tumblr posts with AI partners (e.g. for training): added language confirming use of public content for AI training and added a user-facing opt-out (Settings > Visibility > Prevent third-party sharing).
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Tumblr to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.tumblr.com/policy/en/terms-of-service . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.tumblr.com/policy/en/terms-of-service .

Tumblr is more accommodating on this point. Its updated Terms reference an opt-out under Settings > Visibility > 'Prevent third-party sharing' that withdraws public posts from being shared with AI partners for training. Pinterest's 2024 update added a clause permitting use of public Pin content to train its own AI/ML models for recommendations and safety, without an equivalent Terms-level opt-out. The bot should describe what each document says without giving legal advice.

That being said, the Terms of Service require binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) for disputes like this. If you're not satisfied with their decision regarding your subscription, you may be able to opt out of the arbitration provision within the next 30 days.

5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.tiktok.com/legal/page/us/terms-of-service/en . user_input: If I run a chatbot using Workers AI, can Cloudflare see my users' prompts and use them to train models?
response: No, according to the **"Updated terms"** (effective 2024), Cloudflare clarifies that customer prompts/outputs in Workers AI are not used to train Cloudflare's models.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — CLOUDFLARE SELF-SERVE SUBSCRIPTION AGREEMENT (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Cloudflare and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update added AI Gateway and Workers AI specific terms, clarified that customer prompts/outputs in Workers AI are not used to train Cloudflare's models, and revised acceptable-use rules with stronger anti-scraping/AI-bot abuse language.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Cloudflare to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.cloudflare.com/terms/ . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.cloudflare.com/terms/ .

Cloudflare's infrastructure handles the prompts in transit to fulfil the request, but the Terms place a no-training commitment on Cloudflare's own model development. The bot should describe what the Terms say and remind the user that the underlying model provider's terms may be a separate question.

If your account is deleted, the Terms of Service don't mention what you can do in that situation. If you're concerned about account deletion, you may want to review any backup data you have for your account.

As for your best legal strategy, the Terms of Service mention binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) as the way ChirpSocial's disputes will be resolved. They also require you to file any disputes within one year after the incident occurs.

Ultimately, the Terms of Service say that California law will apply to disputes, and these will be decided in a California court (although this would be done through binding arbitration as mentioned earlier, which may take place remotely, but the governing law is California).
